name: KmStrSearch (Windows kernel UTF-8 and UTF-16 substring search)
baseline: Windows kernel CRT strstr and wcsstr (MSVC runtime; not glibc or musl)
workload: Single match near the end of a buffer (40 B to 1 MB for 8-bit, 80 B to 2 MB for 16-bit) and a worst-case mismatched dense text (repetitive partial matches), run through a multi-threaded kernel driver harness; hybrid Boyer-Moore-Horspool with SWAR, AVX2 and AVX-512BW engines versus CRT.
claimed_speedup: i7-1165G7, 8-bit, GB/s (CRT baseline vs Smart Auto): 10 KB 22.38 vs 45.71, 1 MB 22.66 vs 85.93; 16-bit 20 KB 26.67 vs 68.43. Worse on small buffers: 40 B 3.61 vs 1.95, 256 B 15.03 vs 4.88. README: on mismatched dense text CRT collapses to 0.21-0.37 GB/s while the hybrid delivers 49-81 GB/s, 'up to 385x faster'.
tradeoffs: Windows kernel-mode (WDK driver) code: routes small buffers to a SWAR path to avoid the KeSaveExtendedProcessorState cost of entering vector mode, and uses AVX2/AVX-512BW or ARM64 NEON for larger buffers. Uses 8 KB (UTF-16) skip tables allocated from paged pool. Not a user-mode library; the README says user-mode (TestUm) timings cannot be trusted.
caveats: Very new, single-author exploration ('not strictly benchmark-driven during its design'); no repetition counts or variance reported, compiler flags not stated, and throughput comes from a multi-threaded harness built to saturate the memory bus, so GB/s figures are aggregate and not per-call latency. The CRT baseline measures only 1.35-1.67 GB/s on the VMware guest for small to large buffers and to 0.21-0.37 GB/s on dense mismatches, which reflects that CRT implementation, not glibc/musl (glibc uses a two-way algorithm for long needles). Loses to CRT on tiny and small buffers. Kernel driver telemetry only; no independent reproduction.

name: STOKE
baseline: gcc -O3 and icc -O3 compiled x86-64 code (output quality); expert hand-written assembly for some kernels; Google Native Client's shipped libc string functions in the 2017 paper
workload: Runtime of superoptimized loop-free x86-64 kernels (OpenSSL big-number Montgomery multiplication, Hacker's Delight, SAXPY, linked-list traversal) starting from llvm -O0 code, and 13 libc string functions from NaCl newlib.
claimed_speedup: ASPLOS 2013 paper (PDF opened): the Montgomery multiplication kernel from OpenSSL's big-number library is 16 lines shorter and 1.6x faster than gcc -O3 output and slightly faster than expert handwritten assembly; across the benchmark kernels STOKE matches gcc -O3 and icc -O3 starting from llvm -O0 and in several cases exceeds both. ASPLOS 2017 paper (PDF opened): 'median and average speedup of 25% over the libraries shipped by Google' for 13 libc string functions with formal verification. README tutorial: popcount drops from about 1.05 s to about 0.13 s versus a g++ -std=c++11 -O3 -fno-inline build.
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 and icc -O3 baselines (versions not stated in the extracted paper text); gcc-4.9 used in the 2017 paper's translation mode; README tutorial uses g++ -std=c++11 -O3 -fno-inline
hardware: ASPLOS 2013: synthesis and optimization on a cluster of 40 dual-core 1.8 GHz AMD Opterons (machine used for the runtime speedups not identified in the extracted text); ASPLOS 2017: machines with two Intel Xeon E5-2667v2 3.3 GHz processors and 256 GB RAM
tradeoffs: x86-64 only and Intel-microarchitecture oriented. Needs test cases plus bounded or SMT-based equivalence checking, search budgets of tens of minutes per kernel on a cluster, and works best on short loop-free sequences. README: 'STOKE isn't production ready' and 'nobody is actively working on this code base'; it says it is 'not quite at the point where we can take a generic loop and expect to improve gcc/llvm -O3 code'.
caveats: Speedups are on hand-picked small kernels, and the ASPLOS 2013 Figure 11 reports speedup over llvm -O0 with STOKE 'comparable' to gcc -O3 and icc -O3 on many kernels, not always faster. The 2017 baseline is Google's shipped NaCl libc code (already constrained by SFI alignment rules), not a plain gcc -O3 build. A 2022 TU Delft bachelor thesis, seen only as a WebSearch snippet (not opened), reports that STOKE often fails to match gcc -O3 and struggles with loops. Not a benchmark of assemble time. Same repo holds both papers (docs/papers/asplos13.pdf, asplos17.pdf, cacm16.pdf and others).

name: json-as
baseline: JavaScript built-in JSON.parse / JSON.stringify in V8 (also fast-json-parse and assemblyscript-json)
workload: End-to-end JSON deserialize (including allocating the destination object) and serialize throughput in MB/s on small payloads (19 B to 5.5 kB) and nine standard payloads from the yyjson and nativejson-benchmark corpora, with json-as compiled to Wasm by the AssemblyScript compiler (asc) and run in V8.
claimed_speedup: Deserialize, SWAR mode vs built-in JSON in V8: 1,321 vs 568 MB/s (1.1 kB payload), 5,734 vs 1,295 MB/s (5.5 kB payload), 2,196 vs 168 MB/s (108 B payload), 1,056 vs 401 MB/s (52 B alphabet string). Serialize, SIMD mode vs built-in JSON: 7,775 vs 1,062 MB/s (5.5 kB payload), 3,818 vs 696 MB/s (1.1 kB payload). Library comparison on a 5 KiB GitHub-repo payload (deserialize): json-as struct 5,636 MB/s, native JSON 547 MB/s, fast-json-parse 547 MB/s, assemblyscript-json 32 MB/s. Smallest-gain row: 3D Vector (19 B) deserialize, 356-444 vs 83 MB/s across the three typed modes, while the dynamic JSON.Obj path ties built-in JSON on that row (82 vs 83 MB/s). Numbers read from the chart images overview-deserialize.png, overview-serialize.png and library-deserialize.png on the docs branch (v1.5.0).
tradeoffs: Typed, schema-driven (struct) API: the build-time transform generates a specialised serializer per @json class, so it only competes with JSON.parse when the schema is known up front; dynamic JSON.Obj path is slower. Needs AssemblyScript toolchain and a Wasm host; builds use --noAssert and --uncheckedBehavior always, which removes bounds and assert checks. SIMD mode needs Wasm SIMD support.
caveats: Chart values are only in PNG/SVG images (read from the PNG), not in a text table. The JS baseline parses to generic JavaScript objects while json-as parses into typed structs, so work done differs. Per-row wins vary: JSON.Obj (dynamic) path is not always faster (Alphabet and UUIDv4 rows show 0, 3D Vector 82 vs 83 MB/s). Benchmark author is the library author. Chart footer shows a date of Jul 17 2026 and commit 0bb47d4; later commits exist on main.
